speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CLARIFICATION BY MR. SPEAKER OF RULING MADE ON NOVEMBER 14, 1977
speechtext:
Order, please. Before calling motions pursuant to Standing Order 43,1 wonder if 1 might endeavour to borrow a moment of the time of the House to refer to some remarks which I made yesterday during the course of a ruling on the question of privilege raised by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
After I had decided on the question of privilege raised earlier by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the right hon. Prime Minister raised a question concerning some alleged comments connected with a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 earlier in the day. I rather quickly set that aside-upon reflection, perhaps a little too quickly. In any case, that was set aside yesterday, and I do not propose to return to it.
My concern, first of all, is that I had expressed the view that since the complaint raised by the right hon. Prime Minister yesterday was part of a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ought not to deal with it in the same way as I might those other areas of discussion which were subject to the strictures I referred to in the ruling yesterday. In fact, I was not entirely correct in that, because the sum and the substance of the complaint was not in the motion but in the preamble.
In any case, it occurs to me that I may very well have given an impression that motions and preambles to motions are somehow exempt from the strictures I have put on language used in debate according to the citations to which I referred yesterday. If I have done that, I want to hasten today to correct that impression, because it is quite wrong.
If in the past I have been in the habit of adopting and accepting a sort of self-policing feature about motions pursuant to Standing Order 43, I hope the House will understand that since there has been a limited time for the presentation of these motions, I have tended very much to allow them to police themselves in terms of aspects which might offend or come close to offending some of the rules. Sometimes I simply brush them aside and do not put the question, and I have not examined them with close scrutiny with respect to the opprobrious or unparliamentary language provisions.
I should like to refer to Standing Order 51 which reads as follows:
Whenever Mr. Speaker is of the opinion that a motion offered to the House is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall apprise the House thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the Standing Order or authority applicable to the case.
Furthermore, Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, at citation 199(3) reads as follows:
If the language of a motion is offensive either to the House, or to any member, the same proceedings may be had in relation to it as are proper in the case of disorderly or offensive words used in debate; and, for the same cause, a motion may either be refused an entry among the minutes, or if already entered, may be expunged.
Thus, I think I should make it clear to the House that if I created the impression in a somewhat peremptory answer yesterday to the point raised by the right hon. Prime Minister, that all motions pursuant to Standing Order 43 enjoy some exemption from the strictures against unparliamentary or opprobrious language, that was an incorrect impression. I hope the House will accept my penitence for having done so yesterday and my desire to correct the record as quickly as possible, before even taking any proposed motions pursuant to Standing Order 43 today.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF DECISION TO MAINTAIN WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS-MOTION UNDER S.O.
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF DECISION TO MAINTAIN WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS-MOTION UNDER S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. With inflation of over nine per cent this year and unemployment levels of over eight per cent, giving a combined misery index of more than 17 per cent, confirming that wage and price controls are not only not working but are also adding to our jobless ranks, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That there be an immediate reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs with respect to the government's decision to maintain wage and price controls for most of next year and with respect to the government's attempt to enforce a six per cent ceiling on wage increases, which appears to be based on its forecast of a six per cent inflation level next year, a forecast not shared by independent economists.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Recognizing and respecting the fact that it is in the best interests of the dairy industry, producers and consumers alike, that the national dairy policy, with some modification, continue; however, in view of the fact that a very dangerous impasse has developed between the federal government and the fluid milk producers of Quebec and that in addition dissatisfaction continues throughout most of the participating provinces, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):
That the Minister of Agriculture call together immediately a meeting of all provincial ministers of agriculture along with representatives of all provincial milk marketing boards to resolve these ongoing difficulties and to reach a decision which is mutually acceptable to all.

PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF LOSS OF MEDICAL DOCTORS TO UNITED STATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. From 1974 until 1977, Canada lost 1,500 medical school graduates to the United States. The cause of this emigration lies in the increasing frustration of Canadian doctors with governmental and bureaucratic interference in the medical profession on the federal and provincial levels as well as with the prospect of better income in the United States.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco):
That this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs for study and report to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
According to confidential information, it seems that thousands of applications for Canadian citizenship from ethnic groups are pending, and especially that the files of Quebeckers are knowingly and voluntarily withheld by some Ottawa officials, so as to deprive those future Canadians of a sacred right, the right to vote. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Jean (Mr. Smith):
That an inquiry be immediately undertaken by the Secretary of State to clarify this deplorable situation and that action be taken against the officials found guilty of such a misdeed.

ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR BELIEVING LEVEL OF INFLATION NEXT YEAR WILL BE SIX PER CENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Figures released today by Statistics Canada show that inflation in 1977 so far is rising at an annual rate of more than nine per cent. As the Prime Minister knows, his government has proposed a six per cent wage ceiling this year and next year as far as our workers are

November 15, 1977
Oral Questions
concerned. Since prices are rising so much faster than wages, is the Prime Minister aware that the average Canadian family may well lose $300 in buying power if it is held to a six per cent wage ceiling and inflation continues? If the Prime Minister is aware of this would he indicate to the House why he believes inflation will only be six per cent next year or does he not care if the Canadian worker loses such buying power?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR BELIEVING LEVEL OF INFLATION NEXT YEAR WILL BE SIX PER CENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have indicated in the budgetary speeches and economic speeches that we expect next year the cost of living index will go up at a rate of six per cent or less. That is still our expectation. We do not take the pessimistic projection that the hon. member has in mind as being true.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY MANUFACTURING SALES TAX MIGHT BE RESCINDED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Since the policies of this administration have led to the unique state of rising inflation and rising unemployment, would the Minister of Finance consider waiving the manufacturing sales tax that the government now imposes in order to encourage consumer demand and at the same time lower prices with respect to the predictions concerned?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY MANUFACTURING SALES TAX MIGHT BE RESCINDED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we discussed the possibility with the provinces a few weeks ago of lowering-

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY MANUFACTURING SALES TAX MIGHT BE RESCINDED
speechtext: I was asking about the federal manufacturing tax.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY MANUFACTURING SALES TAX MIGHT BE RESCINDED
speechtext: We did discuss that and only the province of Ontario was willing to go along with the proposition that if the provinces were to cut their sales tax by one per cent we would help them with the other per cent, but there were no other takers. We have looked at the possibility of cutting the federal sales tax, but this was not judged a very good means because we were afraid that the benefits would not be passed on to the consumer. Instead of that, I have decided to cut, for January and February, income tax for people of medium and lower income by the amount of $100.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DECISION TO ALLOW CONTROLS TO CONTINUE NEXT YEAR
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DECISION TO ALLOW CONTROLS TO CONTINUE NEXT YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary is again directed to the Minister of Finance, who must realize that as far as the federal manufacturing sales

tax is concerned a rebate could certainly be made over the next six months. In view of the fact that we do have rising inflation, which would indicate that the controls program is not working-in fact, the controls program has been counter productive in that our jobless ranks are always swelling-would the Minister of Finance reconsider his decision to allow controls to continue well into next year and end controls at least before the end of this calendar year?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DECISION TO ALLOW CONTROLS TO CONTINUE NEXT YEAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that this would have exactly the opposite effect. Had it not been for controls in the last two years, we would be in an even worse position than we are now, and I do not think that the inflation indicator released today will make me change my mind as regards removing the controls by April 14. This confirms that I made the right decision when I made my speech on the economy.

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, and I am interested in his last reply. The Americans are doing much, much better without controls. My question is this. What have his officials told him in regard to what proportion of the current inflation is a result of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar?

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to know exactly what percentage of inflation at this time is due to the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. I do not know exactly how to quantify it, but it is certainly a factor. The report released this morning says, for instance, that higher housing costs are due to the rate increase in municipal and provincial taxes. And it is an area on which we have no control.

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Given the fact that his own officials have stated that probably about 25 per cent of our inflation rate is due to devaluation, what steps is the Minister of Finance taking to try to make Canadian industry more competitive or, indeed, to stop the continuing devaluation of the Canadian dollar? Has the minister talked to provincial governments about borrowing abroad? Has the minister considered any restrictions on travel abroad? What is the minister going to do to try to stop this balance of payments problem and the devaluation of the dollar which is contributing so much to our inflation and to unemployment?

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like the hon. member to read the speeches of two ministers of finance who are not
November 15, 1977

supposed to be necessarily my friends, the ministers of finance of Ontario and Quebec, who have said that devaluation of the dollar at this time was probably something which was good for the manufacturing sector of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext: A final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the Minister of Finance did not understand my question, which was very simple. What is the minister going to do to improve the balance of payments problem and to stop the continuing devaluation of the dollar, which everybody knows is having an incredible effect upon the rate of inflation in this nation?

subsubtopic: PROPORTION OF INFLATION RESULTING FROM DEVALUATION OF DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very surprised that the hon. member does not understand that devaluation of the Canadian dollar is making Canadian products more competitive in the world. It is very basic to the economy. I would be very surprised if in the past he taught his students something else.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST WAGE INCREASES EQUAL INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING AND PROPOSED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE DENIED
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST WAGE INCREASES EQUAL INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING AND PROPOSED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE DENIED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. No economic analysis group outside the government, whether we are talking about the Conference Board, U of T economists or labour groups, agrees that inflation will be held down to six per cent next year. In fact, most of them say it will be a minimum of eight per cent. The minister's own tax reduction of the grand sum of $100 will still mean, with the present rate of inflation, a net loss of $350 per family at the $15,000 level next year. The minister said a minute ago that he is prepared to gamble. Will he remove the gamble for Canadian workers, modify his program and permit increases in wages and salaries next year which will at least be commensurate with the cost of living?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST WAGE INCREASES EQUAL INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING AND PROPOSED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE DENIED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be appropriate to change our economic policy just now. I am of course disappointed with the rate of inflation for this month. On the other hand, I am sure this problem would have been a lot easier to solve if only we could have obtained last August the voluntary support of management and labour, which would have enabled Canada to gain a more favourable competitive position on world markets. Unfortunately we have been unable to convince labour to co-operate with us.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST WAGE INCREASES EQUAL INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING AND PROPOSED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE DENIED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister is at least consistent. Liberals never let facts get in the way of their policy. The government has already agreed that the oil companies will be permitted to increase the price of oil on January I by $1 a barrel. This will mean an increase in the cost for every

Canadian who drives a car and heats a family home. As well, it will result in the loss of some 25,000 to 30,000 jobs on the basis of past experience. Will the minister take steps now to stop that January 1 increase in the price of oil?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST WAGE INCREASES EQUAL INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING AND PROPOSED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE DENIED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this policy was established a long time ago. At the time of the increase in oil prices by the OPEC nations, we decided that rather than Canadians having to take the brunt of it in one shot, we would phase in the increase over a period of years. That policy, which was approved by all parties in the House at that time, has to be lived with today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for-

I should like to put a question to the Minister of Agriculture or, in his absence, to his parliamentary secretary. As a result of the problems experienced by fluid milk producers who are having a hard time getting their subsidies since May, the chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission wrote recently to my colleague from Kamouraska that as long as members of the federation were accused of false representations, those cheques would not be sent out.
Can the parliamentary secretary tell us whether the attitude of the government and the Canadian Dairy Commission has changed and what he intends to do in this specific instance?

November 15, 1977

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Caron (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN PAYMENT OF SUBSIDIES TO FLUID MILK PRODUCERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following the many representations made by the hon. members on this side of the House, I am pleased to indicate that both federations, that is the Quebec Industrial Milk Producers Federation and the Canadian Dairy Commission have reached an agreement on the payment of subsidies. The officials of the Commission are now in the process of figuring out the subsidies for the months of July, August and September. subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: A question for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: ALLEGED "BUGGING" OF MEMBERS' OFFICES-STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Order, please. As I have already indicated to the House, I received advice by letter dated November 3, 1977, from the Leader of the Opposition that a discovery had been made by consultants retained by him that a telephone in the offices of the Leader of the Opposition had been altered in such a way as to make it capable of becoming an eavesdropping device. I asked that the equipment be examined by experts from Bell Canada. I received their report yesterday. While there is some disagreement with respect to the manner in which the device could be used, there is agreement that the telephone had at some time been altered so that it could have been capable of use as an eavesdropping device.
I will not attempt to paraphrase the reports, because in our conversation yesterday afternoon the Leader of the Opposition and I agreed that both reports ought to be tabled, and I will do so immediately. We also agreed that I ought forthwith to invite the Ottawa police to extend the investigation in which they are presently involved to include this occurrence, and I am instructing them accordingly.

speechtext:
I am told by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) that it takes a while. It has certainly taken her some while.
I think it appropriate, as we begin this debate on the motion now before the House of Commons, to note the quite surprising change in atmosphere evident today on the government side, particularly after the Prime Minister of Canada was forced, with his customary graciousness, to withdraw remarks which he made yesterday. I think it is clear to us all how painful it is for the Prime Minister to have to admit that he was wrong. I think it would be quite appropriate for me to say, on this first anniversary of the election in the province of Quebec of a government formed by a party which the Prime Minister declared dead, that the Prime Minister had better get used to the pain of being wrong.
As Your Honour knows, this is the first allotted day in this new session, and there are a number of matters which we on this side of the House could have chosen to raise in this debate. Current economic problems are serious and they show no sign of improving under the policies of this government. We have very serious problems in regard to national unity in this country, problems which were dramatized one year ago today by the election of the Parti Quebecois government, as well as problems regarding which there has been a signal lack of positive response or initiative by the government of Canada in the intervening years.
All of these, sir, are very important questions which could have commanded our attention on this day, but we have decided that it is of utmost importance for this parliament to deal today with the fundamental question of ministerial responsibility and with the refusal of ministers on the other side of this House to accept their responsibility in matters relating to the national security activities of the government of Canada.
I raised this matter in an adjournment debate a week ago. My colleague, the leader of the New Democratic Party, attempted to raise a similar matter yesterday, on privilege. It is a matter which is of fundamental importance to the House. I will not repeat the number of learned authorities which have been cited previously, because I think that the House of Commons accepts the practice of parliament both in the past and today that a minister cannot blame his officials when things go wrong, that the people who are responsible are the ministers of the Crown, not their officials.

November 15, 1977
Security
We raise this point, Mr. Speaker, because if we destroy that principle of ministerial responsibility we destroy the system of government which we have in this country. Our system says that the people of Canada elect members of parliament. Some members of parliament become members of the government, ministers of the Crown, but they answer to the rest of us for all-I emphasize the word "all"-the actions of the government.
The signal fact which has become clear in these last days is that these ministers will not answer for the actions of their government when those actions have been in violation of the law and practice of this country. I remind the House of what has gone on in the last couple of weeks. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), the man who was solicitor general of Canada at the time of the break-in in 1973, sat silent in his place throughout the long debate when this matter was first raised under special order of this House.
In the case of the APLQ break-in, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), the solicitor general of that day, deliberately declined to ask questions which he should have asked and which he knew he should have asked, because he wanted to remain technically ignorant of matters which he had a responsibility to know about. The present Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) admits that he has regular briefings, but he never seems to be told anything. We do not know, of course, what kind of questions the minister asks, and we might never know in this parliament because the cabinet refuses to tell the House of Commons anything.
Now, sir, in a very ominous development the government has prepared the way to give the royal commission of inquiry only a limited story, a partial story, as to the role of ministers in this affair. As reported at page 684 of Hansard, when answering my questions about the nature of testimony concerning the role of ministers to be given to the McDonald royal commission of inquiry, the Prime Minister had this to say:
-there may be some areas which must be kept secret and we would be guided by the law officers of the Crown in that regard.
Two things are important here, Mr. Speaker. One minor matter, except that it falls into the pattern, is that the government itself is not even accepting the responsibility of saying what should be secret and what should not be secret. It is passing that responsibility on to public servants so that the government can blame them if they are found out to be wrong. But what is more ominous, because it raises questions about the adequacy of the evidence before the McDonald royal commission, is that the government of Canada is preparing the way to limit the testimony which it gives concerning the role of ministers of the Crown in all these activities.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, in our system ministers have a larger duty than just to ask occasional questions at briefings. Ministers have a duty to oversee the general work of their departments. This matter has been debated before, so I will quote my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who in 1969, when the Mackenzie report was tabled in the House, had this to say:

It would be completely unacceptable for the House to have the security operations of this country put beyond the knowledge of the Prime Minister or the responsible minister of the government.
That makes clear the fact that ministers have an obligation to ensure that they know what is going on. On November 2, as reported at page 563 of Hansard, he pretended, when we asked him questions about general supervision of what the security service was doing, that he was being asked to begin monitoring the day to day operations of the police, asking them about their information, how they got it and who they got it from. As the distinguished journalist, Mr. W. A. Wilson, has pointed out, the present Solicitor General has apparently been limiting his own questions to security officials by the form in which he puts them. I quote Mr. Wilson:
By the form of his questions stipulating acts that "ought to be brought to my attention," Mr. Fox left it to the RCMP to decide what he should know.
They may have been guilty of very bad judgment in saying no, but that is not the same thing as lying to their minister.

Ministers have been derelict in their duty to supervise.

November 15, 1977

The line the government is putting out is that the people in the field are the culprits, the people who carried out the policy. But, sir, what about the ministers who set the policy? What about the ministers who have a duty to supervise policy? In our system they, too, are responsible. Indeed, they, above all, are responsible for what is done by the public servants under their direction. But this government is doing everything it can to protect the ministers and to blame the civil servants- whether those civil servants are Mounties, members of the security service or whatever.
What must alarm this House, what threatens the very basis of our system of responsible government, is that this is not the first time ministers of this government have blamed civil servants in order to escape responsibility themselves. In the case of the Lockheed affair, the government of Canada accepted millions of dollars of obligations on the basis that it had an oral agreement with Lockheed that would provide interim financing. The minister responsible for drafting the contract complained that one public servant did not reveal that it was simply an oral agreement. He blamed it on the public servant and, in so doing, seemed to suggest that this person, this public servant, stood between the minister and knowledge of: first, what was going on in an interdepartmental task force; second, what was going on in the head of his colleague, the then minister of national defence; and third, what was going on in the entire defence structure of the government of Canada. That was all the fault of one civil servant: it was not the minister's fault, of course!
We saw it again in the case of Atomic Energy of Canada where the minister responsible ducked, ran and tried to leave responsibility fully with civil servants. We saw in the Rudnicki affair. I remind the House that Mr. Rudnicki was fired from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the stated reason of showing a cabinet document to the Native Council of Canada, the group for whom he was supposed to be working. He was finally exonerated by the courts after a trial which indicated that the confusion about the document was the fault of his superiors. But the victim was the civil servant on the scene.

The point stands and remains that whatever the agency, these are civil servants who are acting under the direction of the government of Canada. The illegal actions we have heard about in the last several weeks did not just happen. They were not the result of a wild night on the town. They were done because civil servants thought they had orders to do them.
In his remarks on October 28 in this House, the Solicitor General referred to what he called the "political and social climate prevailing in 1973". I think it would be very worth while to examine that climate. Let us remember, sir, that we are speaking of 1973-not 1970. In the fall of 1970, the government believed there was a state of what was called at the time "apprehended insurrection" in the country. That view, presumably, led the government to give one set of orders to security officers which had to do with the FLQ. But that climate had changed markedly between the fall of 1970 and January of 1973. The Solicitor General might not think so, but his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), stated the reality which most Canadians accept when she said at Carleton University with reference to that time, January, 1973:
There is no way somebody is going to tell me that as a Quebecker there was a state of national emergency somewhere in Quebec and some threats to God knows what. I never perceived anything like that.
The point is this: just as she did not perceive any unusual political climate at that time, neither did anybody else. The question is whether the government of Canada, the political minister who had sounded the alert in the fall of 1970, did their duty and changed their policy instructions to the security service in the time between the October crisis and the break-in in January, 1973. Let there be no mistake about this: the ministers of the Crown had a duty to tell the security service that the mandate had changed because the climate had changed.

need for secrecy involved in any kind of security activities. That is a very genuine and important dilemma. It is one I would welcome the opportunity to have this House discuss.

There has been no action on these matters. I received a one-time offer from the Prime Minister to have one briefing on some aspects of security matters. That was in response to letters that I wrote. In our system, the government must accept responsibility. Today, and too frequently in the past, the
November 15, 1977

ministers of this government have refused to accept responsibility. Instead, they blame somebody else. Parliament must have the power and the information with which to hold ministers accountable. Today, because of the refusal to come clean by ministers on the other side, we do not have that kind of information.
Some surprising and troubling things have happened to parliament in the last decade. Ten years ago we in this House had the power to control spending by the government of Canada. In the years in which this government has been in office, this House of Commons has lost that power to control spending. Throughout the life of this government there has been a refusal to add to the powers of private members, to add to the powers of committees and to make this place more effective. Often, ironically, that refusal has been defended by some reference to ministerial responsibility.
We have had further evidence in the past few weeks that the fundamental principle of a parliamentary system, the principle that ministers are responsible for the actions of their departments, is being broken down gradually, steadily and-in this case, sadly-dramatically. Ministerial responsibility must be restored. If the government will not restore it, parliament has an obligation to do what it can to restore it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this motion. It is a serious motion, one that goes to the root of the problem in a way that the government, through its actions since the opening of parliament, has completely failed to do. I want to discuss two aspects of the motion. The first and most important one is ministerial responsibility which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has emphasized and which I raised in a question of privilege yesterday. The other aspect that I will be speaking on will be expressed concretely in the form of an amendment to the motion. That pertains to the important question of the rule of law.
On the question of ministerial accountability I shall take only a minute or so because I do not wish to repeat arguments I made in the House yesterday, nor do I wish to repeat some of the points the Leader of the Opposition made so well today. The people who are ultimately responsible for what takes place in the ministry of the Solicitor General, that of Justice, or that of Health and Welfare, are not civil servants, whether deputy ministers or the lowest ranking clerks in the department. The
Security
people who are responsible, in a parliamentary democracy, are the ministers.
There is one group of people today which has forgotten that principle in a way which puts all others to shame by comparison. I refer to the cabinet. I quoted yesterday examples from Jennings and from Dawson, two constitutional authorities- and I could add others-pointing out that the notion of ministerial responsibility does not mean a minister needs to have a day to day knowledge of what is going on in every section of his department. What it does mean is that he assumes responsibility for broad policy and the orientation of the law as administered by the department and that, in particular, when something goes wrong he should be ready to correct it promptly. This is the attitude which has been totally absent from the performance of the government and, in particular, totally absent from the performance of three successive solicitors general.
As I say, I do not intend to deal with this aspect at any length because it has been already discussed by the Leader of the Opposition and because I raised it in the House yesterday. Nevertheless, it is something which is essential to parliamentary democracy, and there has been complete failure on the part of the government, and particularly on the part of the Solicitor General, to recognize its responsibility in this area.
I wish to deal today with a broader question as one living, not in the thirties in Germany or in the seventies in Russia but as a Canadian who lives in a society which is basically free, overwhelmingly democratic, overwhelmingly civil libertarian. I address myself this afternoon to the response made by the government when it learned that there had been wrongdoing on the part of a minority in the RCMP and elsewhere in the security services. When I sit back and think of what happened in the United States a couple of years ago, I am scandalized by the response of this government.
Hon. members will recall that the Watergate inquiry, which ultimately led to the resignation of a president, came about because of revelations of spying upon a political party-one political party spying on another. At the time the issue was raised by Senator McGovern, a presidential candidate, the affair was dismissed as having little importance. Indeed, the reaction in the United States was not dissimilar to the reaction here in Canada to the issue we are presently discussing. On one hand, there was a tendency to dismiss it as a trifling thing, if it occurred, and on the other there was reluctance to criticize because of the supposed sanctity of the entities involved. In the United States, for example, people were asking themselves: How is it conceivable that the presidency itself could have allowed such a thing to occur, or actively direct it?
Here, in Canada, I would remind hon. members it has not simply been a case of one political party monitoring another. What we have before us is evidence of the commission of a number of crimes-crimes committed by the RCMP, I regret to say, involving the burning of property, the theft of property, spying illegally upon a political party, and the opening of mail which is categorically forbidden under the Post Office Act. We have learned, too, of "Operation 300," an illegal operation

November 15, 1977
Security
with respect to which the minister said the other day the allegations were substantially correct. These revelations in 1977 in Canada came on top of disclosures that certain security forces or branches of the RCMP or other security forces were spying on Canadian farmers in the National Farmers Union, spying on members of my political party, spying on all kinds of innocent Canadians democratically exercising their rights in a free society.
What has been the response of the government of Canada that dares to call itself Liberal? What has been its reaction to these revelations about burning, about theft, about spying on farmers, trade unionists and political opponents? Have we heard voices from small "1" liberals in the party which history links with the name of John Stuart Mill, saying, "This has got to stop. We are administratively responsible for a number of these things because they have come about through our failure to prevent them"? Did members opposite acknowledge their responsibility and take prompt action to put a categorical stop to it? What have they done? That is the question I want to deal with.
Mr. Speaker, the response has been a debasement of Canadian politics. You would have to go back a long way in Canadian history to see a worse one. First, we got misleading comparisons and phony information provided by a number of ministers. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) used the wonderful analogy that sometimes it is necessary to break the law; that on occasion one had to drive at 80 miles an hour to catch a thief. Then we heard the "spirit of the times" argument- another gem! How John Stuart Mill would have laughed to have heard this argument seriously put forward.
It was left to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to blurt out the truth in the course of an address to students at Carleton University-that in 1973 the spirit of the times was anything but violent; that it was certainly not an atmosphere which would have justified the breaking of the law if, indeed, that is ever justified. Another tactic of the government, arguments having failed, was to attack the opposition. The Conservative party and my own party were attacked for raising questions about civil liberties. We were attacked for suggesting that criminal wrongdoing by the police was every bit as wrong as criminal wrongdoing by other citizens. We were criticized for having the audacity to suggest that it was the government itself which was finally responsible for ensuring that the police obey the law like everyone else.
We heard a perfect example of that attitude in the speech given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to his Liberal cohorts in Vancouver over the weekend. He foamed at the mouth, I am sure, in his castigation of the terrible opposition parties who had dared to criticize the failure of the government; and he introduced a red herring by saying we had been critical of the RCMP. He knows, if he is honest, that we have been critical, on this side of the House, of the complete failure of his government to make sure the RCMP performs correctly.

There was a third device used by this great Liberal government, and that was the suggestion that such illegalities or moral wrongdoings were really carried out in the context of dealing with terrorists. Time after time we heard statements from a variety of ministers that they had to deal with violent groups in society. Extremism in defence of liberty is no vice, according to this government. This is wrong, in terms of their factual suggestions.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, rhetorically: Is the New Democratic Party a party committed to violence, and does it warrant spying upon? Is the Canadian Union of Public Employees, the largest union in Canada, representing working people in every community across the land, the kind of institution that should be spied upon? Is the National Farmers Union of Canada, representative of farmers in half a dozen provinces, the kind of institution that should be spied upon? Is the Quebec Federation of Labour, an institution organized by workers to work for the benefit of the working people in the province of Quebec, the kind of institution that should be spied upon?

speechtext:
In spite of the severe criticism of the RCMP in the past few weeks at the hands of the loyal opposition, I believe Canadians and the government retain great confidence in the force and the manner in which, generally speaking, they have conducted themselves in carrying out their responsibilities.
There are two parts to the motion introduced by the hon. Leader of the Opposition. The first part deals with ministerial responsibility for national security and the national security service. By convention, the responsibility for national security devolves upon the Prime Minister and is shared with those ministers charged with specific responsibility for the police, external relations and the administration of justice.
In part, the government accepted the Mackenzie recommendations in relation to the structure and the responsibility of the security service. It is responsible to a designated minister, the Solicitor General. The head, the director-general, has the right of direct access to the Prime Minister, and the head has a high degree of independence as recommended by the MacKenzie commission. I refer hon. members to recommendation 277(b), page 106 of the Mackenzie report. Also, the government accepted that the security service should become a more clearly recognized, separate and distinct element of the RCMP since there is a clear distinction between the operation-
Security
al work of the security service and that of the police force. On June 26, 1969, the Prime Minister said the following in this House:
It is therefore the government's intention, with the full understanding of the RCMP, to ensure that the Directorate of Security and Intelligence will grow and develop as a distinct and identifiable element within the basic structure of the force, and will be more responsive, in its composition and character, to the national security requirements described by the commissioners... The security service, under the Commissioner of the RCMP, will be increasingly separate in structure and civilian in nature.
As far as policy and operational responsibilities are concerned there is, of course, by positive decision of the government, a very clear line of distinction between responsibility for the policy under which the security service operates and responsibility for the direction of the operations of the security service. That, I understand, is also a position approved of by the Leader of the Opposition-a distinction between policy guidelines and the day to day activities of the RCMP.
The political level, of course, has responsibility for the over-all policy guidance and mandate of the force, and while the security service has some form of operational independence from the political level under policy guidance, the government is convinced that this distinction is right and should be maintained. If I understand the Leader of the Opposition correctly, that is also his position. In that broad context, the commissioner and the director-general of the security service are involved in the over-all operational direction of the security service. The director-general has exercised delegated responsibility for operational policy of the security service.
The government believes that to exercise direction over the day to day operations-in other words, to assume direct operational control over the security service-would be counter to the basic principle of the independence of the police to which we have strongly subscribed for many years. The government has subscribed to this principle in order to make clear that there must not be any possibility of the use of executive authority to influence the work of security and intelligence agencies for partisan political purposes.
We all know from recent painful experiences elsewhere that where executive partisan control is exercised over security and intelligence services, there can be perversion of them for partisan purposes. Watergate is past, but not forgotten. The other thing Watergate showed us is that if there is political intervention in operations and perversion of them for partisan purposes, the involvement of the political level can make disclosure and investigation very difficult. There can be the cover-up of activities or the suppression of information because they involve activities at the executive level. It seems to me that it is, therefore, a great disservice to the country and to services such as the RCMP and the security service to suggest or imply that they have been involved in a Watergate. They have not, and they do not deserve the slur.
Any suggestion that the government should take responsibility for operational control of the security service is one which if implemented could lead to the very situation that was

November 15, 1977
Security
Watergate. We prefer to be judged responsible on the basis of the policy guidance given to the service by the government and by the initiatives we take in relation to the legal framework that governs the operations of the service. In that regard, we continue to examine our policies and the legal framework under which operations are conducted for which we in the government are responsible. We take our responsibilities seriously, as is clearly demonstrated in the initiatives taken in respect of the policy direction given the force and in relation to laws which govern us all.
I would like to enumerate approximately 15 instances of policy guidance given to the force over the years. This has been a matter of continuing attention and concern to this government, especially since the royal commission on security reported in 1969. However, even before that commission reported, the government of Mr. Pearson took steps. In 1963 that government enunciated the security threat and effected procedures to protect the individual and to define the role of the RCMP in the security screening process. In 1966 responsibility for the RCMP was transferred to the Solicitor General from the Department of Justice, to ensure more comprehensive and intensive attention to law enforcement.
In 1966 the royal commission on security was established. In 1969 the report of the royal commission on security was tabled and a number of points were emphasized. Some of these points were that Canada remained a security target and that security should remain the responsibility of the RCMP, but in the context of an increasingly separate and civilian security service. In 1971 the then solicitor general announced the formation of a planning and research group in his ministry to provide civilian analysis and advice on internal security matters. In 1972 the committee structure reporting to the cabinet committee on security and intelligence was restructured. In 1974 the government proposed legislation to govern wiretapping to ensure protection of the individual and to ensure control by the minister responsible of wiretapping where legitimate reason for it was established. Prior to 1974 there was the implementation of those powers by the then solicitor general.
In 1975 and 1976 the government provided guidelines for the security service and clarification of those guidelines in the context of separatist activities. There was the establishment of the Marin commission of inquiry, which reported in 1976. In March of 1977 there was the establishment of an operational review committee. In-camera briefings were offered to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs over the past few years, including this year. A letter was written to the Leader of the Opposition this year offering him briefings on the matter of security.
Finally, this year a commission of inquiry to investigate evidence of illegal activity by the security service was established to advise on policy and procedures of the RCMP and on the adequacy of the law relating to security. Those are approximately 15 measures which have been taken over the years, all for the purpose of ensuring greater policy direction by, and accountability to, the government, the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General.

It is this aspect of the problem that is being emphasized by the opposition, and in my view there is a very difficult problem here for which we must find a solution. I do not think the solution can be found in the simplistic criticism that the government must be responsible for the detailed operational activity undertaken by the security service in trying to ensure national security. However, there is a challenge for the future. In any human organization there is surely room for improvement. That applies to the Tory party and to the NDP as well as to the RCMP, although in the case of the opposition parties to which I referred, the reasons are more self-evident.
I believe we must arrive at decisions on a series of complex policy and legal issues in order to ensure that police operations can and will be carried on within provisions and procedures authorized by law; to decide to what extent the law may have to be changed to permit measures that are considered necessary to combat terrorism, organized crime, espionage and other matters of that kind; and to ensure that our decisions are consistent with the protection of basic and fundamental rights and freedoms of the individual. We must ensure these things while still preserving the independence of police operations from possible political intervention, but with ministerial control of policy. The issues are very important for the country and our society as a whole, but we must not undermine or make impossible the effective work by the RCMP in order to have quick, dramatic and possibly wrong solutions.
In the second part of his motion the Leader of the Opposition also proposes the establishment of a parliamentary committee to look at ministerial responsibility in directing the security forces. I make the following points: first, the government has already established a commission of inquiry concerning the activities of the RCMP. The opposition frequently demanded this. It seems to me advisable to await the report and advice of the commission. The commission can call before it whoever it wishes. In his letter to the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister also pointed out that the government is prepared to discuss questions and issues related to the security service in in-camera sessions of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Such in-camera sessions were held in 1973, 1974 and 1975, and offers for such sessions were extended in 1976 and 1977, but as yet those offers have not been taken up, undoubtedly for valid reasons, by members of that committee.
November 15, 1977

The Prime Minister also offered to the Leader of the Opposition briefings on the state of security in this country. However, the procedure in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs provided an opportunity to members from both sides of the House to raise questions about the general application of security policy. I am, of course, always amazed to see the questions asked by members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, particularly on the police and security side, administered by the Solicitor General, come back up in the House without reference to the fact that questions have been asked systematically by people in this organization and very detailed answers have been furnished in the past, as they will be this year if it is the wish of the parliamentary committee to so examine the estimates of my department in connection with the police and security analysis group.
I should also point out to the Leader of the Opposition that the royal commission of 1966 came to the conclusion that detailed scrutiny of the policies and operations of security agencies was the responsibility of the executive and should not be entrusted to a parliamentary committee. That is not to say that we are not willing to have a look at the over-all policy within the confines of the in-camera examination by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that all the measures that have been taken, there were almost 15 of them, show to what extent the government has seriously taken its responsibilities to ensure control over a mandate given to the security services of Canada. I believe, Mr. Speaker, and I am convinced that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) will agree with me, that nobody in Canada would wish that a government, be it this one or any other, have control over the day to day operations of the Canadian police forces. It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that if such were the case, we would have in fact a political force and a political police in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition said that nobody ever suggested that. None the less, Mr. Speaker, I suggest hon. members on the other side should look over the statements they have made over the past few months. On a number of occasions, they accused us of having a political police which is supposed to prepare lists of enemies of the system; yet, Mr. Speaker, they are accusing us today of not having the police forces in Canada under control. Either we have them under full control, or we do not have them under control at all.
I am saying to the House today that we do not intend to watch over the day to day operations of the Canadian police forces. No government in this country, whether federal or provincial, need control the day to day operations of our police forces; the function of any elected representative is to define a clear mandate for the police forces and see to it that this
Security
mandate is carried out. Through the setting up of some 14 or 15 elements of solution, of control, since 1963, I have demonstrated to what extent the government is aware of this problem, and it goes without saying that there is room for improvement in any human organization. If the control mechanisms and the legislation must be improved, we will improve them.
I would like to stress one thing because hon: members opposite have too often insisted on the fact that we want to amend the legislation and legalize what was illegal, but basically, Mr. Speaker, we have always very clearly established that a security service, a police force generally must act in accordance with the law, the Criminal Code and other federal and provincial statutes.
We have stated, however, that it was clear today that there are some gaps in that legislation. We have reached a point where it would be necessary in an airport such as Mirabel to put up signs which would read as follows: Would terrorists please report to such or such counter. Surely that situation would be quite ridiculous. We think it is necessary to have a security service in spite of the fine words we heard from the leader of the New Democratic Party.

They are certainly getting a name across Canada, and parliament is being smeared accordingly. I must compliment him on his capacity to speak at length but convey no information. That is something worthy of the finest traditions of his two predecessors.
Today the Solicitor General set out what has been done. He says, "We have been doing things." Apparently what has been done has not been very effective. Going back to the earliest days of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country, he left the House this afternoon with such speed that he might have been mounted on a motorcycle again. This is one occasion

when he who is responsible for the security of Canada should be in the House, even to listen to that which he does not fully appreciate, understand or is willing to hear. It just amazes me.
Now, sir, what do we have? We have a continual endeavour on the part of this government to smear the Mounted Police. As far as I am concerned, I will have none of it. I have known the Mounted Police since the days of the territories when they went west to what had been Fort Carlton in 1903, when the force was called the Northwest Mounted Police. Later on it became the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, I think in 1904, and finally in 1919 it assumed its present name. Let not any member think that people on the prairies will ever countenance in the slightest the contemptuous innuendoes which have been directed at the Mounted Police. If there has been wrongdoing, then, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, the responsibility is with the government of this country, and nowhere else.
I mentioned the Mounted Police because I saw the force in those days as a boy. We were living 17 miles from the nearest village on the old Edmonton-Carlton-Winnipeg trail. The Mounted Police had come there, proud of their traditions. When there was crime committed, they sought out the alleged wrongdoer. When he was brought to trial, he was prosecuted by a member of the Mounted Police, generally a sergeant. He was often tried before an inspector of the Mounted Police. In all the years during those early days of the settlement of western Canada, no one-except in one or two isolated cases- ever denied that justice was being done. The Mounted Police endeavoured to ensure justice and to maintain it.
From the time I became a member of the bar in 1919-I was a member of the bar in all three western provinces-until 1957 I had many cases. With the exception of two individuals, the Mounted Police believed in their slogan "Maintain the right". But today, in consequence of the actions of this government in endeavouring to bring about the suspicion that what has been done is wrong and was due to the Mounted Police, I need only point out that none of these things happened until the government of Canada decided to place security under certain civilians. Since then some things have been done which cannot be justified.
Why was security removed from RCMP? I am beginning to wonder whether this was part of a plan to put an end to the Mounted Police. I have already said that going back to the 1940s the Prime Minister has had a disregard for the Mounted Police which I am not going to detail in his absence, though he will immediately recollect what I have in mind.
What is the situation today, Mr. Speaker? The Solicitor General has given the House an explanation. Where are the other former solicitors general? Where is "Go-go Goyer"? He is in Africa endeavouring to establish some kind of Francophone combine. Why is he not here? There was not such a rush that he should leave at this time. The hon. gentleman opposite will disqualify himself for cabinet rank unless he watches out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion for debate today deals with a most important matter of course, but we have been debating it for over two weeks now. The motion reads, and I quote:
That this House... deeply regrets its (the government's) unwillingness to allow a committee of this House to study the role of ministers in security operations.
I feel that we should know the truth about the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and every other police corps in Canada, about its methods of inquiry and procedures in enforcing law and order in Canada. All police forces must operate according to the law and order of the land, within well defined guidelines. Their task is very tricky in that they must enforce law and order while respecting the freedoms of every individual.
Mr. Speaker, I remember when I was very young how we used to read in the newspapers that, for instance, the RCMP or the Mounted Police, as we used to call them in those days, were above reproach and always got their man. We were proud of that police force and rightly so, I would think, in those days; but today and especially more recently, every attempt has been made to belittle that police force; I sometimes wonder just how successful those attempts have been.
However, Mr. Speaker, in their operations to fight against organized crime in Canada, the police must not abuse their rights, and the government must see to it that they do not. Over seven centuries ago, Bracton expressed this principle-it is true that in those days he spoke of the king, but today we could speak of government. Here is Bracton's principle:
The King himself must not be answerable to Man, but to God and the Law, because the Law makes the King. In consequence, let the King give the Law what the Law gives him, that is authority and power, for where the will and not the Law constitutes authority there is no King.
November 15, 1977

It could be said today that if the will takes precedence over the law, democracy is in jeopardy. Closer to us, the then Speaker of the House of Commons, Dr. Gaspard Fauteux, said: "In the Canadian democracy, the state is the servant of the individual and in all other forms of government, the individual is the servant of the state." However, we can avoid lapsing into these other forms of government where individual rights are relinquished to the almighty state. According to Ralph W. Page, democracy promises liberty to all and to everyone an opportunity to manage his own self improvement. It is based on the principle that man is not a machine and that his destiny is not based upon the accumulation of material goods but on his understanding of moral and spiritual values and on his self-improvement in this field. This is the kind of democracy we want to safeguard.
We do not want to lapse into that kind of regime where one half of the population watches the other half. In a well governed democratic society, the law abiding citizen has nothing to fear. He may eat, sleep, work and entertain himself in peace. He may have his conscience at rest, secure in the conviction that he and his family are safe, provided they all abide by the law. He may even expect certain things from society such as those he is entitled to under the law. He does not have to fear the torture chamber, the concentration camp, the execution squad, the confiscation of his property or the loss of his citizenship, but in all other societies one must be ready for the worst.
The Canadian citizen must be able to address himself to his provincial or federal representative to express to him his desires, make representations or voice his complaints without feeling that he is being spied upon. Civic study circles must be able to reach the same ends by making known the opinions of more important groups without being spied upon. This is what I am asking from this government and at last the Solicitor General seems to have understood that it is necessary to monitor more closely the actions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to prevent that police force from turning into an SS corps devoted to the service of a tyrant. In a free country such as Canada, the existence of laws and their implementation imply as a necessary corollary the existence of order. In the absence of any kinds of laws or when the existing laws are not observed, then the law of the jungle will prevail. When order does not exist, nothing will prevent attacks against the freedom of the majority of the citizens. This is why law and order have become almost synonymous. This expression conveys a single identical concept.
Mr. Speaker, parliament must have the right to inquire and have its say in the ways laws have to be applied; this right must not be surrendered exclusively to the government's discretion. As history shows, every time men have neglected to restrict the powers of their rulers, their powers have been increased at the expenses of the people governed. Every time governments have acquired unlimited powers, they have turned into tyrannies. The duty of Parliament is to preserve democracy and no police force whatsoever should have the right to commit illegal actions to further its ends. We have instituted
Security
an inquiry commission, the McDonald Commission, to throw the light on all aspects of the issues raised by the actions of the RCMP.
The RCMP is not blameless and efforts are being made to destroy it piece by piece. In certain sectors, this police force has been nearly completely depreciated. Honest Canadians feel that they need an authority to enforce the law and what should this authority be if not a respected police force? We are not faultless. There is much work to be done. The police must deal with organized crime. There are underground organizations for drug distribution, people who smuggle liquor and other goods, betting syndicates, prostitution chains, gangs of murderers; there is also bribery and corruption since without it very few illegal organizations can survive. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is very busy.
Drug trafficking is prohibited by law, but when we see how easy it is for young people even in high schools to obtain all sorts of drugs, we wonder what the RCMP is doing. I would certainly be in favour of establishing a committee to study the role of ministers in security operations, but this committee should have all the powers of a royal inquiry commission to call on all the witnesses that the committee will deem necessary to hear and these witnesses should testify under oath. This is very serious. But we already have a royal commission. If this commission is not empowered to investigate the role of ministers in security operations, we should extend the mandate of the McDonald Commission.
The House of Commons has many other matters to deal with. We are aware of the problems of unemployment, inflation, energy and housing. We must ensure a guaranteed minimum income for all Canadians. We must pass as soon as possible some legislation to improve the lot of small and medium businesses in Canada. We have urgent economic problems to solve in Canada. We should not let the government be sidetracked to minor issues.
Since the beginning of the present session, we have not really dealt with concrete matters; we have talked at length of the future of the Canadian constitution, of the problems caused by the Parti Quebecois. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in this
November 15, 1977

important debate, during the course of my remarks I should like to deal with some of the historic and perhaps constitutional questions involved in the evolution of security and of the RCMP in this country.
It has become obvious to all of us over the years that in examining principles of ministerial responsibility, or the lack of it, with particular reference to security, which is covered in this motion, how unnecessary the growth of undesirable or misguided security methods were, had the government acted conscientiously and efficiently on the report of the Mackenzie Royal Commission on Security tabled approximately ten years ago. Also, it is obvious how stubborn and perverse this government has been over a long period of time in refusing to be frank with parliament, even when it became evident to some of us that something in security matters was going terribly wrong.
Responsible ministers, which include not only solicitors general, were either curiously anxious not to know what was going on, or they lacked any desire to correct the situation. Therefore the present conditions are caused, in a large part, by the negligence and shortsightedness of ministers of the Crown and are exacerbated by the indiscriminate use of section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act, which has roused the ire of the chief law enforcement officers of the provinces who resent the withholding of information which is rightfully, in their opinion, within their jurisdiction.
Another element has been the complacency of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who said on February 7, 1977, when I questioned him about government files on millions of Canadians and the necessity of providing Canadians with access to their files and more freedom of information, the following:
I for one as a Canadian would not admit we have lesser rights than the Americans. They may have more abuses there and that is why, perhaps, they have to have corrective measures.
It appears the Prime Minister's conclusions were wrong. Since that day we have seen that we need corrective measures as well. It was obvious to many of us, apparently before it was obvious to the right hon. Prime Minister.
Security matters in this country, besides being in a state of disarray because of poor judgment and lack of attention on the part of the government, are also complicated by very real constitutional problems. 1 am sure the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) and the Minister of Justice are very aware of that.
Both the Attorney General of Canada and the Solicitor General of Canada are concerned with the operations of security. While 1 would not attempt to specify all of the powers possessed by these ministries, there is a doubt as to whether their powers extend into the administration of justice given to the provinces by section 92(14) of the British North America Act.
If such powers do not extend into this widely defined provincial prerogative, serious difficulties arise; one must look at the Official Secrets Act, for example, before prosecution can be entered, the authority of the Attorney General of Canada is required. An examination of this act clearly reveals that it comes within the meaning of the administration of
Security
justice. Furthermore, certain offences contained therein are duplicated in the Criminal Code, which is the responsibility of the provinces. In the latter instance, no such authority for prosecution is required. I wonder precisely where the Attorney General of Canada legally derives his power to override provincial jurisdiction. Also this act provides authority to appoint persons with the powers of peace officers, with no jurisdictional limitations imposed by order of the governor in council. I am not satisfied where it is clearly specified in the law that the governor in council can override the exclusive powers of the provinces in the field of the administration of justice.
We should consider as well another very important statute as far as civil rights in this country are concerned, which is the Protection of Privacy Act. The definition of subversive activity in that statute is very interesting. I seem to recall, when the term itself was put forward, that it was met with opposition. I suspect it was returned to the authorities to come up with some more acceptable forms of definition which finally found its way into the act. If we examine the definition of this term and translate the actions into offences, practically every one will be contained in the Criminal Code. This means that subversive activity also comes within provincial jurisdiction, yet it is the Solicitor General who is responsible for issuing warrants.
This matter requires some explanation. It has been suggested over the years that an assumption has grown up without challenge that the RCMP is constitutionally responsible for national security or internal security, although both terms have no real meaning in law. The only term I can find is "peace and order", and certainly the RCMP is not by definition responsible for that, although they have been its foremost defenders over the years. The assumption has wormed its way into this act as it has into the Official Secrets Act, and if it cannot be substantiated by constitutional law, it can be establishing a very dangerous precedent.
One must take a very hard look at whether the role of a security service should include an enforcement function. Perhaps to be consistent, if it is to be a federal responsibility, it should not have this power, which brings it back into an even more apparent conflict on jurisdictional grounds.
I believe that parliament should seriously consider that the term "defence", set out in section 91(7) of the British North America Act, should be defined to include the term "security intelligence" which should also be defined. This would place the matter firmly at the federal level and overcome the jurisdictional problems which are inherent at this time.
I think it is obvious as well at this point that military intelligence activities, by virtue of section 91(7), have a far clearer and more legitimate function than the security activities of the RCMP, and this to my mind is an unfortunate situation. If section 91(7) were amended in this way, the Solicitor General would be on firm legal ground for the issuance of warrants under the Protection of Privacy Act.
While parliament may legislate laws for peace and order, I submit that it has constitutionally no power to administer

Logically it seemed a bit irregular, I suggest, for parliament to have a statutory police act in these circumstances, but years ago it did just that when it enacted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, which provides authority for members of the RCMP to be appointed peace officers in every part of Canada, thereby allowing unlimited jurisdiction, which again provides the provinces with a good constitutional argument.
